title: GCSE Biology Practice Paper 1
summary: Foundation and crossover · grades 1 to 5 · 24 questions · 36 min

questions.question: Which part of a cell controls which substances enter and leave it?
questions.explanation: The cell membrane controls the passage of substances in and out of the cell. The cell wall, found in plant and bacterial cells, strengthens the cell.

questions.question: What is diffusion?
options: The movement of water only across a membrane
The movement of particles against a concentration gradient, using energy
The movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration
The net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the spreading out of particles, giving a net movement from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated. It needs no energy from the cell.

questions.question: Which part of a cell is the site of protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: Proteins are made on ribosomes. Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration happens, and chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens.

questions.question: What is the process called by which a cell becomes specialised for a particular job?
questions.explanation: Differentiation is when a cell gains the structures it needs to carry out a particular function. Most animal cells differentiate early in development, but many plant cells keep the ability throughout life.

questions.question: Which organ produces bile?
questions.explanation: Bile is made in the liver. It is stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine.

questions.question: Which reagent is used to test for starch, and what colour shows that starch is present?
questions.explanation: Iodine solution changes from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present. Benedict's solution is used for sugars and Biuret reagent for proteins.

questions.question: Which plant tissue transports dissolved sugars around the plant?
questions.explanation: Phloem carries dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant. This is called translocation. Xylem carries water and mineral ions up from the roots.

questions.question: Why do veins contain valves?
options: To make the blood flow faster
To let oxygen diffuse out of the blood
questions.explanation: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves are needed to keep it flowing towards the heart and stop it flowing backwards.

questions.question: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
questions.explanation: Measles is caused by a virus and is spread by droplets from sneezes and coughs. Malaria is caused by a protist, gonorrhoea by a bacterium and athlete's foot by a fungus.

questions.question: Which of these is a non-specific defence of the human body against pathogens?
options: The skin acting as a barrier
questions.explanation: Non-specific defences stop any pathogen getting in. They include the skin, hairs and mucus in the nose, and acid in the stomach. Antibodies are specific to one pathogen.

questions.question: In which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs the light energy needed for photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares aerobic and anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
options: Only aerobic respiration produces lactic acid
Anaerobic respiration transfers more energy per glucose molecule
Aerobic respiration does not need oxygen
Only anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid
questions.explanation: Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid and transfers much less energy. Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question: What is homeostasis?
options: The response of an organism to a stimulus
The production of hormones by glands
Keeping the body's internal conditions within set limits
The transport of substances in the blood
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions, such as body temperature, blood glucose and water levels, to keep them at the best levels for cells and enzymes to work.

questions.question: How are hormones carried around the body?
options: In the air in the lungs
questions.explanation: Hormones are chemicals released by glands directly into the bloodstream. They travel in the blood plasma to their target organs, so their effects are slower than nerve impulses.

questions.question: How does a contraceptive pill containing oestrogen and progesterone prevent pregnancy?
options: It forms a barrier at the cervix
It makes the lining of the uterus thicker
It stops FSH production, so no eggs mature
questions.explanation: The hormones in the pill inhibit the production of FSH, so eggs do not mature and are not released. Spermicides kill sperm, and barrier methods stop sperm reaching the egg.

questions.question: What is a change in the environment that an organism can detect called?
questions.explanation: A stimulus is a change in the environment, such as light, sound or temperature. Receptors detect stimuli, and effectors bring about the response.

questions.question: In the nervous system, what are effectors?
options: Muscles or glands that bring about a response
questions.explanation: Effectors are muscles, which contract, and glands, which release hormones. They respond to impulses carried by motor neurones.

questions.question: Which molecule carries the genetic information in cells?
questions.explanation: Genetic information is carried by DNA, which is found in chromosomes in the nucleus. DNA is a polymer made of two strands twisted into a double helix.

questions.question: What is a dominant allele?
options: An allele that is only expressed when two copies are present
An allele that is expressed even if only one copy is present
An allele that is found only in males
An allele that always causes a disorder
questions.explanation: A dominant allele shows its effect when just one copy is present. A recessive allele only shows its effect when two copies are present.

questions.question: In a species, brown eyes (B) is dominant to blue eyes (b). Two heterozygous parents (Bb) have children. What is the expected ratio of brown-eyed to blue-eyed offspring?
questions.explanation: The possible offspring are BB, Bb, Bb and bb. Three of the four have at least one B allele and have brown eyes, and one is bb with blue eyes. The ratio is 3 : 1.

questions.question: What is a change in the DNA sequence of a gene called?
questions.explanation: A mutation is a change in DNA. Mutations happen all the time. Most have no effect, but occasionally one gives a new characteristic that helps an organism survive.

questions.question: Which of these could cause a species to become extinct?
options: An increase in its food supply
questions.explanation: Extinction can be caused by new diseases, new predators, new competitors, or changes to the environment that happen faster than the species can adapt.

questions.question: What do the arrows in a food chain show?
options: The transfer of energy and biomass from one organism to the next
questions.explanation: Each arrow points from the organism being eaten to the organism that eats it. It shows the direction in which biomass and energy are transferred.

questions.question: Which of these helps to maintain or increase biodiversity?
questions.explanation: Breeding programmes protect endangered species. Other helpful measures include protecting habitats, replanting hedgerows and reducing deforestation. The other choices all reduce biodiversity.
